An element only has one `onclick`. Assigning to it silently replaces any handler that other code put there. `addEventListener()` adds a handler alongside the others, and it takes options such as `once` and `signal`.

The rule reports any assignment to a property named `on` plus a DOM event, no matter what the object is.

{/* Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit this section. */}

## Configure

Off by default. To turn it on:

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"unicorn/prefer-add-event-listener" = "error" # or "warn"
```

{/* End of the generated section. */}

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad {"count": 2} */}
```js
button.onclick = () => save(form);

window.onload = null;
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
const onClick = () => save(form);
button.addEventListener("click", onClick);

button.removeEventListener("click", onClick);
```

Reading the property is fine, and so is a name that isn't a DOM event:

{/* good */}
```js
if (button.onclick) {
  button.click();
}

player.onscore = update;
```

## When not to use it

Some objects aren't event targets, and a property such as `onmessage` or `onerror` is the only way to give them a handler. Turn the rule off for the files that use them.
